nodes.label: Ocean Currents
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Continuous, directed movement of ocean water. Caused by wind, Coriolis force, temperature and salinity differences, and ocean floor topography. Warm currents flow from equator toward poles; cold currents from poles toward equator. Move clockwise in Northern Hemisphere, counterclockwise in Southern Hemisphere (subtropical gyres).

nodes.label: Warm Ocean Currents
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Currents carrying warm water from tropical to higher latitudes along eastern margins of continents. Include Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift, Kuroshio Current, Brazil Current, Agulhas Current, and East Australian Current. Moderate the climate of adjacent coastal areas making them warmer. Bring moisture and rainfall.

nodes.label: Cold Ocean Currents
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Currents carrying cold water from polar to tropical regions along western margins of continents. Include Canary, Benguela, Peru (Humboldt), California, and Labrador Currents. Create dry conditions on adjacent coasts contributing to coastal deserts (Namib, Atacama). Produce fog but little rainfall. Support rich fishing grounds due to upwelling.

nodes.label: Peru (Humboldt) Current
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Cold current flowing northward along the western coast of South America. Creates extremely dry conditions on the Peruvian and Chilean coast (Atacama Desert). Supports one of the world's richest fisheries through upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water. El Nino disrupts this current causing collapse of fisheries.

nodes.label: Benguela Current
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Cold current flowing northward along the southwestern coast of Africa. Contributes to the aridity of the Namib Desert. Rich fishing grounds due to upwelling. Part of the South Atlantic subtropical gyre. Similar to the Humboldt Current on the opposite side of the Atlantic.

nodes.label: Kuroshio Current
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Warm current flowing northward along the eastern coast of Japan. Pacific equivalent of the Gulf Stream. Moderates the climate of Japan. Meets the cold Oyashio Current in the northwestern Pacific, creating productive fishing grounds. Also called the Japan Current. Second strongest current after the Gulf Stream.

nodes.label: Upwelling
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process where cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep ocean rises to the surface. Caused by offshore winds that push surface water away (Ekman transport), allowing deep water to replace it. Creates productive fishing grounds. Occurs along western coasts of continents. Disrupted during El Nino events.

nodes.label: Thermohaline Circulation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Deep ocean circulation driven by density differences caused by temperature (thermo) and salinity (haline). Cold, salty water sinks in the North Atlantic and flows southward along the ocean floor, eventually rising in the Indian and Pacific oceans. Also called the global conveyor belt. Takes about 1000 years for complete circulation.

nodes.label: Ocean Gyre
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Large system of circular ocean currents formed by wind patterns and Coriolis force. Five major gyres: North Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Pacific, South Pacific, and Indian Ocean. Rotate clockwise in Northern Hemisphere, counterclockwise in Southern. Accumulate floating debris - Great Pacific Garbage Patch in the North Pacific gyre.

nodes.label: Sargasso Sea
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Region in the North Atlantic bounded by ocean currents (Gulf Stream, Canary Current, North Atlantic Drift, North Equatorial Current) rather than land. Named for Sargassum seaweed floating on its surface. Only sea with no land boundary. Calm waters at the center of the North Atlantic gyre. Eel breeding ground.

nodes.label: Labrador Current
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Cold current flowing southward from the Arctic along the eastern coast of Canada. Meeting of cold Labrador Current and warm Gulf Stream off Newfoundland creates dense fog and one of the world's richest fishing grounds (Grand Banks). Carries icebergs southward - the Titanic was sunk in this area.
